title: Reading and the courts, 1830s
hook: Where more young men could read, did fewer crimes reach court? France, 1825-30.

knows: schooling is said to reduce crime
doesNotKnow: that in Guerry's 1830s France the most literate departments recorded more property crime per person, not less

misconception: Where more people could read, less crime was recorded.
objective: The learner can say that in Guerry's record the most literate quarter of French departments recorded about 1.7 times the property crimes per 100,000 people of the least literate quarter (18.9 against 11.3), with crimes against persons the same (5.9), and that this compares departments' court records, not people, and does not show a cause.

claims.text: Where it stops: these are cases brought to court in 1825 to 1830, which depend on policing as well as crime; they compare departments, not people, and two numbers moving together say nothing, alone, about what caused what (reveal).
claims.source: 'Cases brought to court', '1825 to 1830': history-data.mjs guerry 'what' (Crime_pers and Crime_prop = population per crime, Compte général 1825-1830) and the HistData Guerry doc. 'Depend on policing as well as crime': a general limit of court records (wording by cultural-reviewer, culture-en-brief change 1); the fact-checker decides whether it needs a source. 'Compare departments, not people': the table has one row per department. The last clause is a reasoning limit, not a fact about the record.

recall.question: Towns with more libraries report more thefts. What is the safest reading?
options: They go together here; the cause needs more evidence
recall.why: Two things rising together across places can share a cause (bigger, richer towns have more of both); the pattern alone does not say which causes which.
